html:
The day in April 1856 when stonemasons in Melbourne, Australia, stopped work and marched to Parliament to win an eight-hour working day. They were among the first organised workers anywhere to gain it.

In the boom after the Victorian gold rush, building workers were in short supply and so had strong bargaining power. Stonemasons, led by James Stephens and James Galloway, demanded "eight hours labour, eight hours recreation, eight hours rest", a slogan going back to the reformer Robert Owen. On 21 April 1856, masons at the University of Melbourne walked off and marched to Parliament House, then being built. Employers agreed, without loss of pay.

The win was limited to some trades at first, and the eight-hour day spread across Australian industry only slowly over the next decades. The day is still marked by Labour Day holidays in Australia, and the numbers 888 appear on old union banners and monuments. The fight for shorter hours went on around the world, and it is remembered on May Day. See Australia.
sum: The day in April 1856 when stonemasons in Melbourne, Australia, stopped work and marched to Parliament to win an eight-hour working day. They were among the first organised workers anywhere to gain it.
